body:
Sites can set headers to ensure that they never share a browser process with another site. This prevents an attacker from loading sensitive data into memory and then reading it with a side-channel attack or browser exploit.

I propose to add a set of requirements that have the effect of enforcing site isolation, such as requiring Cross-Orgin-Resource-Policy (CORP), Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy (COOP), Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy (COEP) response headers.

- [Post-Spectre Web Development](https://www.w3.org/TR/post-spectre-webdev/)
- [Site Isolation](https://www.chromium.org/Home/chromium-security/site-isolation/)
- [tabnabbing · Issue #1602 · OWASP/ASVS](https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/1602)

ping @Sjord

I think the sites I linked do a good job of explaining the attack scenarios:

1. the attacker's site loads some sensitive content from the victim's site.
2. they read this with a browser exploit or side channel attack.

The first step can often be prevented with same-site cookies. With lax samesite, it is still possible to perform authenticated cross-site GET requests, which is often sufficient to request sensitive information. With strict samesite cookies this is not possible. Also, there can be cases where same-site cookies don't help:

- the attacker has control over a domain that is same-site but not same-origin, or
- the sensitive resource is not protected by cookies, but by basic auth or firewall.

I asked:
> Do you have more precise attack scenario(s) in mind? Then I could validate, is it already covered by requirements or not.
> 
> Related requirements most likely are located in [V50](https://asvs.dev/v5.0.draft/0x50-V50-Web-Frontend-Security/).

And I still have the same question - what scenario is not covered by requirement below?
* V50.3.6 Verify that the Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) Access-Control-Allow-Origin header field is validated against an allowlist of trusted origins. When "Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *" needs to be used, verify that the responses do not include any sensitive information.
* V50.4.3 Verify that the Origin header field is validated against a defined list of allowed origins to match the desired Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) policy.
* V50.5.1 Verify that JSONP functionality is not enabled anywhere across the application to avoid Cross-Site Script Inclusion (XSSI) attacks.
* V50.5.2 Verify that data requiring authorization is not included in script resource responses, like JavaScript files, to prevent Cross-Site Script Inclusion (XSSI) attacks.


> they read this with a browser exploit or side channel attack.

browser exploit I consider to be out of scope for ASVS.
@elarlang Related also to #2481, I am going to do some research into some practical scenarios that may not be covered by the requirements listed. Will report back in a few days...
ping @ryarmst - any news?

@elarlang Yes, I can provide some updates, but this has been a long journey and it continues...

My first simple conclusion: I have not seen any attack articulated that Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy (COEP) mitigates. Outside of very obscure scenarios I can conjure up (specific and unlikely application functionality), I cannot conceive of an immediate value, so I will not discuss it further. I am open to practical examples if anyone can provide any. 

As part of this research, I revisited tabnabbing (and reverse tabnabbing). Unlike `<a>` and related tags, `window.open()` by default will provide a reference to the opening window (even cross-origin) via `window.opener` (same Browsing Context Group - BCG). Reverse tabnabbing is possible in this scenario (one exception: Firefox seems to restrict access to the opener object cross-origin in this case). I made a video demonstrating this behavior across browsers and will upload when I have some time... Likewise, a site acting as an opener can use `window.open()` to open other cross-origin targets within the same BCG. In addition to tabnabbing-type attacks, both scenarios can also lead to XS-leaks. 

One relevant XS-leak example is this [old Facebook Graph API attack](https://www.imperva.com/blog/archive/facebook-privacy-bug). I believe Facebook has mitigated this with Fetch Metadata validation (and perhaps other controls). The attack is quite simple, really: an attacker's site uses `window.open()` to target Facebook's Graph API with a specific search query and because positive search results are embedded in iframes, the attacking page can use the window reference to get the _frames.length_ which returns the number of iframe elements within the opened Facebook page. 

Now to review existing requirements. The most relevant section is V50.4, but the chapter doesn't have perfectly logical sectioning. First, at a high level, I think the definition of sensitive functionality may be too imprecise (forgive me, I don't recall the last issue this was discussed):

> Sensitive functionality in this context could include accepting form posts for authenticated and non-authenticated users (such as an authentication request), state changing operations, resource-demanding functionality (such as data export), etc.

It's not clear to me that "sensitive functionality" here ought to include requests that can be simple GET requests to retrieve resources (as in the Facebook Graph API example). A CORS exception is not needed in this case, because information is not read directly, but inferred from accessible properties. Even if we assume "sensitive functionality" includes these types of requests (or expand the definition to make it clear), I do not think the present requirements in V50.4 are sufficient. The closest would be 50.4.1, which is for "CORS-safelisted" requests:

> [MODIFIED, MOVED FROM 4.2.2, COVERS 13.2.3] Verify that CORS-safelisted requests to sensitive functionality are checked to ensure that they originate from the application itself. This may be done by using and validating anti-forgery tokens or requiring extra HTTP headers that are not CORS-safelisted request-headers. This is to defend against browser-based request forgery attacks, commonly known as cross-site request forgery (CSRF).

While the proposed protections (CSRF tokens or a header) would mitigate an XS-leak attack such as the one against Facebook, it also adds an additional possible vector for information leakage depending on its implementation: an attacker may be able to infer a user's session status based on the behavior of the application. The handling of (response to) an unauthenticated user may be different than how the app handles a missing CSRF token/header. This would be a much more minor leak, but is a leak nevertheless.

Further, no existing requirement appears to mitigate reverse tabnabbing through `window.open()`, which can still occur in at least Chromium-based browsers (maybe not all). While this is a separate attack vector, Cross-Origin Opener Policy (COOP) mitigates both of these scenarios by isolating the protected website in its own BCG. This also may have secondary benefits in further mitigating the potential of speculative execution side-channel attacks, but I have to admit that this is outside my expertise (though worth noting there are [occasionally new viable vectors](https://predictors.fail/) in this space).

Therefore, I think it would be worthwhile to add a requirement to set a strict COOP. This is the recommendation from the [XS-Leaks Wiki](https://xsleaks.dev/docs/defenses/opt-in/coop/):

> If possible, it is recommended to set `same-origin`. If you set `same-origin-allow-popups`, be sure to review what websites you open with window.open and ensure that they are trusted.

I don't think there is an existing relevant requirement, so I will propose some starting text:

> Verify that every HTTP response includes a Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy header to prevent malicious websites from obtaining and abusing window references to the protected application. The directive `same-origin` must be set unless `same-origin-allow-popups` is required and `window.open()` is used only to open trusted documents.

I think there is room for improvement there, but will leave it for now for discussion.

Regarding Cross-Origin Resource Policy (CORP), I think it may be worth integrating with 50.5.2, but it's somewhat broader than XSSI. I think existing requirements are probably sufficient, but I do like it as a defense in depth mechanism. The XS-Leaks Wiki describes CORP as [This is a very strong and highly encouraged protection](https://xsleaks.dev/docs/defenses/opt-in/corp/).

Thank you! That seems like a lot of effort put into it.

I need to play through the provided scenario first to understand the preconditions and impact completely.

When describing the attack scope in this case, it would be helpful when it is always clear is it:

  * only same-origin
  * cross-origin but same-site
  * cross-site (also cross-origin)

Different browsers may have different scoping here.

Previous scoping example: https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/1602#issuecomment-1497104029 && https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/1602#issuecomment-1637654168

---

"Sensitive functionality" in request forgery context - it is a bit of a different topic, and it is probably easier to follow if it is discussed separately. The "name" can be improved, the idea is "the functionality that needs to be protected from request forgery attacks". But by concept it is different impact-family - request forgery is triggering the functionality without caring what the response is, in this case, as I understand, we talk about an information leakage scenario.
This is really amazing feedback @ryarmst - I am considering getting a "Ryan" tattoo on my 🍑 to celebrate your work. Thank you!

@elarlang I will put together a summary table of scope, attacks, and mitigations (hopefully tonight when I have a moment).

Regarding the "type" (or "impact-family") of attacks, it might make sense to break things into the following classifications:
- Write attacks (essentially CSRF) - these cause a state change in the app
- Read attacks (CORS, XSSI, and perhaps others) - these read response data through one or more mechanisms
- Inference/Leak attacks - these are attacks that do not read data from a response but infer it (or infer other characteristics) from exposed properties/behavior

What makes these topics both challenging and related is that the various protection mechanisms are not all attack-specific; many interact and also can be applied to mitigate different attacks. For example Fetch Metadata validation alone could probably meet the needs of many apps to mitigate most attacks. 

@jmanico If you get "Ryan" then I'll get the Manicode logo.

I haven't forgotten about this. @elarlang Regarding attack scope, I have been considering cross-origin (and also cross-site) attacks since 50.1.1 already requires origin separation. 

I have been thinking about what requirements might be needed and how existing requirements might be better structured or written (if necessary). For starters, I organized existing requirements that I thought would be relevant to preventing cross-origin read, write, or leak attacks. Note that the "Relevant Summary" is not necessarily the intent of the requirement referenced, but its relation to these classes of attacks.

| Control                   | #  | Requirement | Requirement Functional Scope | Relevant Summary                                                                                                   |
| ------------------------- | -- | ----------- | ---------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Cache-Control: No-store   | 1  | 8.2.1       | Sensitive/dynamic data       | In addition to preventing storing sensitive information, this prevents cache probing attacks                                                           |
| Correct Content-Type      | 2  | 13.1.7      | All functionality            | Ensure content is set with the correct Content-Type response header (50.3.2 also specifies sniffing protection)                                        |
| SameSite Cookies          | 3  | 50.2.3      | All functionality            | Cookies restricted with SameSite set to Lax or Strict                                                                                                  |
| CORB                      | 4  | 50.3.2      | All functionality            | `nosniff` [expands CORB protections](https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/master/services/network/cross_origin_read_blocking_explainer.md) |
| Anti-Framing              | 5  | 50.3.5      | All functionality            | Prevent page from being framed                                                                                                                         |
| Strict CORS               | 6  | 50.3.6      | All CORS                     | Ensure that implemented CORS policies are strict (validate allow-listed Origins)                                                                       |
| CSRF Tokens               | 7  | 50.4.1      | "sensitive functionality"    | Requires that requests originate from in-app workflow (including patterns like synchronizer, double-submit cookie)                                     |
| No CORS Preflight Bypass  | 8  | 50.4.3      | "sensitive functionality"    | Prevents the application from accepting request types that do not require CORS preflight when it should be required                                    |
| HTTP Request Type         | 9  | 50.4.4      | "sensitive functionality"    | Requiring appropriate non-safe HTTP request methods                                                                                                    |
| Fetch Metadata Validation | 10 | 50.4.4      | "sensitive functionality"    | Validate Sec-Fetch-* headers to ensure appropriate type and origin of request (also referenced in 50.6.1)                                              |
| Origin Validation         | 11 | 50.4.1      | "sensitive functionality"    | Validate the Origin for CORS-safelisted requests                                                                                                       |
| No Sensitive Data in JS   | 12 | 50.5.2      | "Data requiring auth"        | Do not return sensitive dynamic data in JS                                                                                                         |
| CSP: Sandbox              | 13 | 50.6.1      | Renderable content           | Generally renders returned content inert and may also have benefits beyond limiting malicious content execution client-side                            |
| COOP                      | 14 |             |                              | Restrict document to its own browsing content group (BCG)                                                                                              |
| CORP                      | 15 |             |                              | Add restrictions beyond standard SOP to prevent cross-origin rendering of response body                                                                |

I am going to use this as a reference and return with some proposals in relation to actual attacks. I think some warrant new requirements (like number 14 above), whereas I think it is worth considering merging some new controls with existing requirements (for example, I think CORP can be used in requirements like 50.6.1, though I would like to do some testing with it).
Just for to-read list for myself: https://web.archive.org/web/20231101074337/https://www.collinjackson.com/research/papers/appisolation.pdf

Sorry @elarlang I had a post written up here explaining why I broke this into two additional proposals, but it looks like it didn't post. I will see if it's on my other system, but for now I am adding details in each issue...
